title: Granular thermostat implementation within the soft-sphere Discrete Element Method (DEM) framework, considerations and limitations
authors: Marco Previtali, Herbert Eric Huppert, Sergio Andres Galindo Torres
abstract: Dense granular flows are commonly investigated using the soft-sphere Discrete Element Method (DEM), whereas large-scale applications generally require continuum models. Granular temperature, defined as the variance of particle velocity fluctuations, is a relevant variable to collapse rheological scaling. However, experimental forcing approaches used to control temperature also affects other aspects of the granular state.   An alternative is to use a thermostat algorithm to control the fluctuation energy directly. Although thermostat algorithms are well established in Molecular Dynamics (MD), their behaviour in dissipative DEM systems has received comparatively little attention. We show that conventional Langevin and Nosé-Hoover thermostats exhibit complementary limitations: Langevin control requires strong coupling to offset collisional dissipation, thereby damping particle dynamics, whereas Nosé-Hoover does not independently disrupt the correlations and segregation generated by repeated inelastic collisions, leading to non-ergodic and numerically unstable states.   To address these limitations, we introduce two pairwise hybrid formulations combining deterministic temperature regulation with stochastic decorrelation. Both enforce the prescribed temperature, while variation of the stochastic decorrelation timescale modifies velocity statistics and associated mesoscopic properties such as diffusivity. Finally, application to pressure-controlled simple shear shows that increasing granular temperature at fixed inertial number reduces the apparent friction, consistent with previously reported trends. The framework therefore provides controlled reference states for comparing differently forced granular systems and identifying the variables required for temperature-dependent constitutive models.
summary: This paper addresses the difficulty of simulating granular materials by proposing hybrid thermostat algorithms for the Discrete Element Method (DEM). These new methods allow researchers to independently control the granular temperature while also tuning the underlying velocity statistics. This provides a crucial, controlled reference state for developing accurate constitutive models for complex, dissipative systems.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop controlled reference states for studying granular rheology by independently controlling the magnitude of velocity fluctuations (granular temperature) from the statistical character of the forcing.
main_result: The proposed pairwise hybrid formulations successfully enforce a prescribed granular temperature while allowing independent modification of velocity statistics, providing a controlled framework for constitutive model development.
method: The authors introduce two novel pairwise hybrid formulations that combine deterministic temperature regulation with stochastic decorrelation techniques to simulate granular systems.
model_or_system: The study focuses on dense granular flows simulated using the soft-sphere Discrete Element Method (DEM). The system is inherently dissipative, requiring specialized thermostats to maintain controlled energy states.
key_observables: Granular temperature (variance of velocity fluctuations), apparent friction, diffusivity, and velocity statistics.
important_parameters: Inertial number (I), coupling strengths ($\xi_{La}, \xi_{NH}$), and the stochastic decorrelation timescale.
main_assumptions: Conventional thermostats (Langevin, Nosé-Hoover) have limitations: Langevin requires strong coupling, and Nosé-Hoover fails to account for correlations generated by inelastic collisions.
figures_summary: Figure 14 (mentioned in notes) shows the Mean Squared Displacement (MSD) evolution for different thermostats, indicating that the growth is only linear for a limited time window.
paper_structure: The paper analyzes the limitations of existing thermostats (Langevin, Nosé-Hoover) in dissipative DEM systems, introduces the hybrid formulations, and validates the framework by applying it to simple shear flow to study temperature-dependent rheology.
why_interesting: While focused on classical granular physics, the challenges in implementing thermostats—specifically decoupling energy control from correlation structure—are fundamental problems in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics applicable to open quantum systems.
